tickerTips: Tip: Pay yourself first by setting aside 10-20% of any income or allowance immediately.
Smart Habit: Always buy or rent used textbooks to save up to 60% every semester.
Reality Check: Buying a $4 coffee daily costs over $120 a month! Make coffee at home.
Rule of Thumb: Follow the 50/30/20 rule to balance Needs, Wants, and Savings effortlessly.

basicConcepts.title: 1. Income (Money In)
basicConcepts.description: All money you receive during the month. For students, this includes monthly allowance, part-time jobs, scholarships, or freelance work.
basicConcepts.example: Example: $300 monthly allowance + $150 tutoring income = $450 Total Income.

basicConcepts.title: 2. Fixed Expenses
basicConcepts.description: Regular expenses that stay the exact same amount every single month. They are predictable and essential.
basicConcepts.example: Example: Room rent ($150), Monthly bus pass ($40), Internet bill ($25).

basicConcepts.title: 3. Variable Expenses
basicConcepts.description: Expenses that change from month to month based on your spending habits and choices.

basicConcepts.title: 4. Needs vs. Wants
basicConcepts.description: Needs are essential items required to survive and study. Wants are non-essential items that add fun or convenience.
basicConcepts.example: Needs: Meal plan, textbooks. Wants: Gaming subscription, concert ticket.

basicConcepts.title: 5. Savings & Emergency Fund
basicConcepts.description: Money set aside for future goals (e.g. buying a laptop) or unexpected emergencies (e.g. phone repair).
basicConcepts.example: Goal: Save $20 each week = $80 saved per month!

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is considered a Fixed Expense for a college student?
quizQuestions.explanation: Correct! Room rent is fixed because the cost remains identical every month.

quizQuestions.question: According to the 50-30-20 rule, what percentage of your income should go towards Savings?
quizQuestions.explanation: Correct! 20% of income is recommended for building savings and emergency funds.

quizQuestions.question: If you purchase a $5 daily Boba tea, how much will you spend in a 30-day month?
quizQuestions.explanation: Correct! $5 x 30 days = $150 per month on boba tea!

quizQuestions.question: What is an Emergency Fund meant to cover?
options: Buying video games on release day
Unplanned medical bills or urgent laptop repair
Upgrading to a new phone every year
quizQuestions.explanation: Correct! Emergency funds are set aside exclusively for unexpected urgent needs.

moneyMistakesList.title: 1. Impulse Buying & Flash Sales
moneyMistakesList.studentScenario: Rahul sees an online flash sale with 40% discount on a jacket he didn't plan to buy. He spends $60 from his grocery budget.
moneyMistakesList.impact: He runs out of grocery money by the 3rd week of the month.
moneyMistakesList.correctiveAction: Enforce the '48-Hour Rule'. Wait 2 full days before buying non-essential items to see if you still truly need them.

moneyMistakesList.title: 2. Unused & Forgotten Subscriptions
moneyMistakesList.studentScenario: Sara signed up for 4 free trials (streaming, music, gym, fitness app) and forgot to cancel before auto-renewal.
moneyMistakesList.impact: Loses $45 monthly without even using 3 of the services.
moneyMistakesList.correctiveAction: Set calendar reminders on the day you start any free trial to review and cancel if unnecessary.

moneyMistakesList.title: 3. Ignoring Small Daily Expenses ('The Latte Factor')
moneyMistakesList.studentScenario: Alex buys a $4 snack and $3 energy drink every afternoon at the campus canteen without writing it down.
moneyMistakesList.impact: Adds up to $210 per month without Alex realizing where the money went.
moneyMistakesList.correctiveAction: Track every daily purchase in an expense planner, no matter how small.

moneyMistakesList.title: 4. Spending First and Saving 'Whatever is Left'
moneyMistakesList.studentScenario: Zain receives his monthly allowance, spends freely for 3 weeks, and finds $0 remaining to put into savings.
moneyMistakesList.impact: Zero progress on savings goals and stress when unexpected fees pop up.
moneyMistakesList.correctiveAction: Practice 'Pay Yourself First'. Put 20% straight into savings as soon as allowance arrives.

moneyMistakesList.title: 5. Paying Bills Late and Incurring Penalties
moneyMistakesList.studentScenario: David forgets the deadline for his mobile postpaid bill and library fees.
moneyMistakesList.impact: Pays an extra $15 in late fee penalties every month.
moneyMistakesList.correctiveAction: Schedule automatic payment alerts or mark bill due dates on your phone calendar.

chatbotPrompts: What is a need vs a want?
How much should a student save monthly?
How can I stop impulse buying?
How do I create a simple student budget?

chatbotKnowledge.response:
The 50-30-20 rule is a simple budgeting guideline! Divide your monthly allowance or income into:
- 50% for Needs (rent, food, books, transport)
- 30% for Wants (hobbies, outings, streaming)
- 20% for Savings (emergency fund, goals).

Needs are essential items required for survival and education (like meals, rent, textbooks, and health care). Wants are non-essential items that improve comfort or entertainment (like gaming consoles, luxury clothes, and daily cafe drinks).
As a rule of thumb, try saving at least 15% to 20% of whatever income or allowance you receive. Even saving $1 to $2 a day builds financial discipline!

To control impulse buying:
1. Use the 48-Hour Rule before buying non-essentials.
2. Delete saved credit card info from shopping apps.
3. Make a shopping list before going to stores and stick strictly to it!

Starting a budget is easy:
1. Calculate your monthly income or allowance.
2. Deduct your fixed needs (rent, bills, pass).
3. Set aside your savings goal first.
4. Allocate remaining funds for daily food and entertainment!
An emergency fund is money kept strictly for unexpected urgent expenses (like laptop repairs, lost bus pass, or medical visits). Aim to keep around $50-$100 as a student safety net.

contactFaqs.q: Are my budget entries stored on any remote server?
contactFaqs.a: No. All entries, goals, and calculations run completely client-side in your browser for privacy and demonstration.

contactFaqs.q: Can I adjust the 50-30-20 budget ratio?
contactFaqs.a: Absolutely! The 50-30-20 rule is an educational baseline. Students with low expenses can save more, or adjust based on individual needs.
